title: Identity Theft and Credit Fraud
subtitle: Contain the incident before it becomes a paperwork franchise

blocks.text: Identity fraud is the only situation where someone borrows your name and returns it with paperwork.

This course gives you a calm order of steps for suspicious credit activity. Sort out what happened, protect your money and access, save the evidence, report through verified channels, correct both files and watch for the next attempt. Speed matters. Accurate speed matters more than reacting to the first number in a scary text.
Identity theft is stealing personal information. Identity fraud is using it. Exposure is a warning. An account or charge you did not authorize is evidence of misuse.

items.title: “One call to my bank fixes every identity-fraud problem.”
items.text: Your bank can protect its own accounts. But other creditors, both bureaus, the police, the CAFC and government issuers may each have a separate role.

blocks.text: CAFC: Identity theft and fraud
You can respond to suspicious credit activity in the right order, even when you are scared.
blocks.detail: You will know what to secure first and who to tell, so the first number in a frightening text never sets your plan.
blocks.extra: Noah’s story comes next, then Round 2 gives you a first-hour kit.

sections.title: Noah’s Name Had a Very Busy Weekend

blocks.text: Meet Noah
paragraphs: Noah Cardinal is an electrical apprentice in Saskatoon. He is gathering his documents for a new rental.
Then one of his credit reports shows a mobile account and a credit card he never opened. The next morning, a collector calls about the mobile bill.

Next, a “fraud recovery specialist” calls. For a fee, he says, he can erase the accounts, as long as Noah installs remote-access software and pays in cryptocurrency. That is rarely how reputable paperwork says hello.
Noah stops replying, saves every message and starts an incident log instead.

Using official phone numbers, he calls his bank and the providers he does not know. They lock access and give him case numbers. On a trusted device, he secures his email, changes reused passwords and turns on multi-factor authentication.

He asks both credit bureaus for fraud alerts and disputes the accounts. He reports to the police and the CAFC. His SIN may be exposed, so he follows Service Canada guidance and checks his CRA account on the official site.
It takes weeks. One account disappears; the other needs a second package of papers. His rental date moves, but rushing never cost him more money or access.
His name had a very busy weekend. This time, it did not get a second one.

blocks.text: Noah’s incident log tied together every organization, date, case number and next step.
The conclusion
Recovery was not one heroic call. It was five steps: contain, document, report, correct and verify, always through official channels.
You can tell a warning from confirmed fraud before you spend your first hour.
blocks.detail: You will sort exposure from misuse, so you protect the right accounts first and skip the wrong ones.
blocks.extra: Next, Round 1 shows how to sort the signals before you chase any of them.

sections.title: Round 1: Classify the Incident Before You Chase It

blocks.text: A breach notice does not prove a new loan exists. An unknown account, collection call or credit notice deserves a close look right away.

items.title: Accounts, inquiries, addresses, employers or balances you do not know on either credit report.
Missing bills, redirected mail, one-time passcodes you did not ask for or password-reset notices.
Charges, benefits, tax changes or service accounts you did not approve.
Collection calls or credit decisions for an account or application you did not make.
“No money left my bank account, so there is no identity-fraud problem.”
items.text: Fraud may show up first as new credit, a phone plan, redirected benefits or a taken-over account. Check for every kind of misuse, not just your chequing account.

blocks.text: FCAC: Checking reports for errors and fraud
Use a trusted device and official contact details. A suspicious link or phone number is evidence, not directions.
The first-hour response kit

items.title: PROTECT MONEY
items.text: Call affected banks, card issuers or providers. Report activity you did not approve, block cards, secure access and ask them to open an investigation.

items.title: PROTECT ACCESS
items.text: Secure your main email and change any reused passwords. Turn on multi-factor authentication and check recovery addresses, devices and forwarding rules.

items.title: PRESERVE EVIDENCE
items.text: Save messages, screenshots, statements, envelopes, transaction details and call notes before accounts or devices change.

items.title: CHECK BOTH CREDIT FILES
items.text: Get your Equifax and TransUnion reports. Ask both bureaus for a fraud or identity alert and dispute information you do not know.

items.title: CREATE OFFICIAL REPORTS
items.text: Contact your local police and keep the file number. Report to the CAFC online or at 1‑888‑495‑8501.

items.title: PROTECT IDENTITY RECORDS
items.text: If your SIN, CRA account, passport, driver’s licence or health card is involved, follow the issuing office’s official process.

blocks.text: A fraud alert asks lenders to verify more. It helps, but it does not promise that every application will stop.

items.title: “I should delete scam messages immediately.”
items.text: First save the sender details, dates, payment instructions and screenshots. Then follow your provider’s or the police’s advice on safe removal.

blocks.text: Secure your email early. A hacked inbox can reset passwords across banking, phone and government accounts.
CAFC: What to do if you are a victim

sections.title: Round 3: Turn the Incident Into a Case File

blocks.text: Correction can take more than one round. Keep one secure folder with a master log, so each organization gets the evidence it needs and not every private document you own.

items.title: Incident summary
items.text: One paragraph on when you found the activity, which accounts are affected and what you did not authorize.

items.title: Evidence index
items.text: Numbered statements, screenshots, notices and copies of ID. Send copies, and black out what is not needed.

items.title: Case-number register
items.text: The organization, how you reached them, the date, who you spoke to, the case or police number, what they promised and when you follow up.

items.title: Credit correction
items.text: Dispute each account, inquiry, address or balance you do not know with the creditor and with both bureaus where it appears.

items.title: Monitoring calendar
items.text: Check your statements and both files at 30, 60 and 90 days, then at 6 and 12 months, or sooner if new signs appear.

blocks.text: The two bureaus may hold different information. Fixing one file does not prove the other is accurate.

items.title: “A recovery company can guarantee every fraud item will vanish for a fee.”
items.text: Real investigations rely on evidence and official correction processes. No one can guarantee the result, and victims are often targeted by recovery scams.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: You get a breach notice but see no unauthorized activity. Is this exposure or confirmed fraud?
items.detail: Exposure. Treat it as a warning and keep watching. Confirmed misuse needs evidence, such as an account or charge you did not authorize.

items.title: A text says to call right away about a frozen bank account. Which route do you use?
items.detail: Use the number on an official statement or card, or the bank’s website that you find yourself. Do not use the text.

items.title: Why secure your email early?
items.detail: A hacked inbox can reset passwords across banking, phone and government accounts.

items.title: An unknown account shows up on only one report. Who may need your request?
items.detail: The creditor and the bureau that shows it. Still review the other bureau, because the files can differ.

items.title: A recovery expert asks for remote access and cryptocurrency. What is the safest response?
items.detail: Stop contact, do not pay or install anything, save the evidence and verify and report through official channels.

blocks.text: Keep watching after the first fix. Stolen information can be reused months later.

sections.title: Your Action: Build Your First-Hour Response Kit

blocks.text: Fill in only what is safe to store. Use partial references and share only what is needed, through official channels.
A complete incident file means fewer repeated explanations, and every follow-up has an owner, a date and a reference.
Detect, contain, preserve, report, correct and monitor.
blocks.detail: If a step creates new urgency or asks for secrecy, remote access or an unusual payment, pause and verify.

items.title: Identity theft
items.text: Taking someone’s personal information without permission.

items.title: Identity fraud
items.text: Using stolen personal information to pretend to be someone and get money, credit, services or benefits.

items.title: Account takeover
items.text: When someone gets control of an existing account, often through stolen passwords or password resets.

items.title: Fraud alert
items.text: A notice on a credit file that asks lenders to take extra steps to verify who is applying.

items.title: Multi-factor authentication
items.text: A sign-in that needs more than one kind of proof, such as a password and a code from an app.

items.title: Credit inquiry
items.text: A record that someone looked at a credit file. An application inquiry you do not know can be a fraud signal.

items.title: Recovery scam
items.text: A second fraud that promises to win back your losses or erase records in exchange for money, access or personal information.
